articles.draft_title: Public-sector strike suspended after draft deal: what September backdating would mean
articles.draft_description: The proposed pay agreement moves to union ballots. A €45,000 salary example shows the difference between an annual pay rise and arrears paid for part of a year.
articles.draft_body:
The public-sector strike planned for Thursday 12 November has been suspended following overnight agreement on a draft pay deal, according to PA's reporting of the ICTU statement. Members still need to vote on the proposal. Families should check their school or appointment provider's latest notice before changing arrangements.

The first reported pay adjustment is 2% or €1,200, whichever is greater, effective from 1 September 2026. For someone on €45,000 basic annual pay, 2% is €900, so the €1,200 minimum is larger. That would lift the annual rate to €46,200, subject to the final agreement and the employee's circumstances.

The annual increase and the arrears cheque are different amounts. With full-time eligible service and equal monthly accrual, €1,200 a year is €100 gross a month. Four months from September through December would therefore represent €400 gross. This is a transparent budgeting illustration, not confirmation of a payroll date or a guaranteed cheque. Part-time service, changes in grade and payroll rules need individual checking.

The reported 10.75% headline spans the agreement through March 2029 and includes local bargaining. Applying the whole figure to November pay would overstate the immediate change. Before budgeting, check the final salary schedule, ballot result and your employer's implementation notice. The existing take-home-pay calculator can illustrate deductions from a changed annual salary, but cannot determine your arrears entitlement.

This update should replace the current article's 9 November account of the negotiating offer. Preserve the canonical URL and distinguish the older €1,200 negotiating report from the new effective-date schedule.

articles.draft_title: Dublin storage-heater project targets 20 homes: how to judge the savings
articles.draft_body:
A project launched at Camac Crescent in Inchicore connects upgraded storage heaters in 20 homes to surplus renewable electricity. Co-operative Housing Ireland says older heaters have been replaced with Elnur HHR PLUS units linked to EnergyCloud. Heat can be stored when surplus electricity is available and used later.

For households, the financial question is how much purchased electricity the system displaces. An illustrative 100 kWh avoided at a hypothetical 25 cent unit rate would reduce energy charges by €25. If the system instead delivers 100 kWh of extra warmth while paid consumption stays the same, that is a comfort improvement with no corresponding €25 reduction. Neither example estimates this project's results.

A useful assessment would compare metered purchased electricity before and after installation, the tariffs applied and heating comfort, while accounting for weather and household use. The announcement gives no measured saving per home. Residents considering a similar arrangement should ask their housing provider who pays for installation and maintenance, how ordinary paid charging works, and whether the controls preserve their preferred heating schedule.

The launch describes a specific group of homes. A general application route or entitlement to free electricity has not been verified. The project merits follow-up when measured bills, access terms and usable licensed photography are available.
